Q48755950.summary: In this finely carved ivory panel, three veiled women approach from the lower right, greeted by the angel seated before the tomb, a two-storey building crowned by a domed rotunda, while two guards slump against it. Above, the risen Christ, haloed and holding a scroll, strides up a hill and grasps the hand of God reaching from the clouds, as two disciples below cower or look up in awe. It is one of the oldest known figurative images of the Resurrection and Ascension.
facts: The panel was acquired for the Bavarian National Museum in 1860 from the Bamberg collector Martin von Reider, after whom it is named; it is the oldest work on display in the museum (inv. MA 157).
Drill holes at the four corners suggest it was once set into the cover of a liturgical book.
The tomb building has been discussed as a possible reflection of the shrine over Christ's tomb in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, consecrated in 335.
Q48755950.notes: Date c. 400 and origin Rome or Milan per German Wikipedia and the Commons file description; worklist had '4th century'.

Q25503237.summary: A dense crowd of figures fills this continuous frieze. At the left Christ points his rod towards Lazarus, standing swathed in the doorway of a little temple-tomb, while a woman crouches at his feet; in the centre figures holding loaves and baskets on the ground recall the multiplication of the loaves. At the right Abraham grasps the kneeling Isaac, about to sacrifice him, the ram beside the altar.
facts: The sarcophagus was discovered at Auch and is traditionally called the tomb of Saint Clarus.
Wikidata, following the museum's records, lists among its subjects the raising of Lazarus, the feeding of the multitude, the sacrifice of Isaac, Daniel and Adam and Eve.
The photograph is one of the high-resolution images of the Musée Saint-Raymond's collections released under a free licence.
Q25503237.notes: Not every subject listed by Wikidata could be confirmed in the photograph.
Q25503237.original_title: Cuve de sarcophage dite « tombeau de saint Clair »

cur:manuscripts-rossano-cleansing-temple.summary: Under the colonnade of the Temple, Christ in a gold mantle turns toward two white-haired priests who question him, while on the right a money-changer sprawls over his overturned table and traders drive out oxen, sheep and a cage of doves. The Greek heading names the episode of those driven out of the Temple. Beneath, prophets hold up their texts in witness.
facts: The diocesan museum's own list of the miniatures calls this scene the 'talk with the priests of the Temple', reflecting the dialogue on the left that accompanies the expulsion on the right.
Like the other picture pages, it combines a single Gospel event with four prophet portraits whose scrolls carry Old Testament verses.

cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: On a green mountaintop, Christ stands haloed while two black demons try to tempt him and two angels come to minister to him; a vessel, bowl and round loaves lie on the ground. The verse 'he shall give his angels charge over thee … lest thou dash thy foot against a stone' was quoted by the devil in tempting Christ.
facts: The manuscript came to Württemberg under Duke Charles Eugene (its sale is first mentioned in 1787) and has been in the library at Stuttgart since at least 1818.
The Stuttgart Psalter was made around 820–830 at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; its 168 leaves contain the psalms with 316 coloured miniatures set between the verses they illustrate.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature.

princeton:24185.summary: Framed by spirally fluted columns under a low pediment, a curly-haired young shepherd stands with a sheep slung over his shoulders, smiling slightly as he looks out at the viewer. Two more sheep wait at his feet beside two small trees, and a bird perches in the branches at the left. The slab is a clear, confident example of the Good Shepherd as it was carved on Christian sarcophagi around 300, promising the dead the care of the shepherd who seeks out the lost.
facts: The museum notes the shepherd's practical dress: a belted long-sleeved tunic, laced boots and puttees, wrappings that protected the legs from thorny undergrowth.
The slab was probably cut from the centre of a strigilated sarcophagus, where three relief panels were separated by wavy fluting.
It was bought by Princeton from the dealer Piero Tozzi in Rome in 1952.

walters:71.68.summary: Beneath an arch on slender columns Christ hangs on the cross, his body long and still, his head bowed toward his mother. The Virgin at the left raises her hand in sorrow, and St John at the right lifts his hand toward Christ. Once the centre of a triptych, the plaque now sits in a later fabric-covered mount.
facts: The Walters dates the plaque to the second half of the 10th century and notes that it was originally the centre of a triptych.
Henry Walters bought it in 1925 through the Paris dealer Henri Daguerre.
walters:71.68.notes: Image viewed on the Walters image server.

feat:ruthwell-cross.summary: Standing over five metres tall, this Northumbrian cross — probably used as a preaching cross — is carved with scenes from the Gospels, most famously Christ standing in majesty upon two beasts who, as its inscription says, recognised him in the desert as Saviour of the world, and Mary Magdalene drying his feet with her hair. It is among the most ambitious works of early medieval sculpture in Europe, uniting Mediterranean figure carving with Insular vine-scroll ornament and Old English poetry.
facts: Its runic inscriptions contain lines closely related to 'The Dream of the Rood', in which the Cross itself speaks of bearing Christ — among the oldest surviving texts of English poetry, though many scholars think the runes were added somewhat later than the carving.

Around 1642 the cross was broken up under an act of the Church of Scotland's General Assembly against 'idolatrous monuments'; the minister Henry Duncan gathered the fragments, re-erecting them in 1802 and reassembling the cross with a newly carved crossbeam in 1823.
Since 1887 it has stood in a specially built apse inside Ruthwell church, protected from the weather.
Its inscriptions are in both Latin and Anglo-Saxon runes — unusual on a Christian monument — making it a bilingual meditation on Christ.
